text: My Ministerial Statement will address Question Nos 1 to 19 for Oral Answer and Question Nos 45 to 48 for Written Answer at yesterday's Sitting, Question Nos 40 to 42 for Oral Answer and Question No 28 for Written Answer in today's Order Paper, as well as related questions that have been filed for subsequent Sittings.

text: It also resulted in severe damage to rail infrastructure which required extensive repairs over more than five days.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will cover the sequence of events that took place on 25 September and the responses from the Land Transport Authority (LTA) and the public transport operators in the subsequent days.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will do my best to address the questions from Members.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, I seek Members' understanding that as investigations into the incident are still ongoing, some of the details can be determined only after investigations have been completed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the morning of 25 September 2024, at around 9.00 am, SMRT reported a possible fault on train T33, a first-generation KHI train that was travelling eastbound on the East-West Line near Clementi station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SMRT stopped the train at Clementi station, alighted the passengers there for their safety and proceeded to withdraw the train to Ulu Pandan Depot so that train services would not be affected.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To return to the nearest depot at Ulu Pandan from Clementi station, the train had to travel further east to the nearest turnaround track located at Queenstown station, so that it could change onto the westbound track and head back towards the depot.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As the train was travelling west between Dover and Clementi stations, an axle box dislodged from the bogie of one of its cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A bogie is the wheel assembly of a train.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The KHI train is a six-car train and each train car has two bogies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Each bogie has four wheels on two axles and each axle has an axle box on each end.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When one of the axle boxes dislodged from the incident train, it caused the wheels of one bogie to shift to the side of the rail.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As the other 11 bogies of the incident train remained on the rails, the train was able to continue travelling for a few minutes on the rails westbound past Clementi.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At around 9.25 am, when the train reached the reception track leading to the Ulu Pandan Depot, the significant damage to the trackside equipment caused a power trip along parts of the East-West Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a result, the incident train stalled between the reception track and the main line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Four other trains between Clementi and Buona Vista stations also stalled due to the power trip.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Three of these were at stations, where commuters could alight at the platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One of the trains stalled about 40 metres before the platform at Clementi station.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Passengers on this train had to be detrained onto the tracks, guided by SMRT staff, who ensured that all commuters reached the platform safely.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At this point, LTA's crisis management group was activated.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To ensure that commuters could continue their journey, SMRT activated free regular buses within five minutes at around 9.30 am, and bridging buses between Boon Lay and Queenstown stations by 9.50 am.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The bridging buses arrived from 9.58 am onwards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When SMRT staff attempted to restore train service, they realised that extensive damage had been caused to the track and trackside equipment between Dover station and the reception track leading to Ulu Pandan Depot, and it would take time to remove the incident train from the tracks and to carry out the repairs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It would not be possible for trains to pass through this section of the East-West Line before the repairs were completed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To continue service on the rest of the line, westbound trains coming from the city had to be turned around at Queenstown, where a turnaround track is located.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Similarly, eastbound trains coming from Tuas Link had to be turned around at Boon Lay, where there is a turnaround track.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To preserve service along as much of the East-West Line as possible, SMRT decided to run shuttle services, which are trains that travel back and forth along the same track.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The shuttle service continued to be supported by bridging bus services that connected commuters between Queenstown and Boon Lay.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Later in the day, when heavier crowds were observed at Buona Vista station, SMRT adjusted bridging bus operations to focus on the critical stretch between Buona Vista and Jurong East stations that was without train or shuttle services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To support these services, additional spare buses were deployed and some bus captains on rest days were recalled.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Don Wee and Mr Leong Mun Wai asked whether other bus services were affected.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Due to the scale of bridging bus operations, some buses and bus captains had to be redeployed from other lower-demand services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Bus operators determined these redeployments based on ridership and frequencies of their other services, in order to maintain service standards and minimise inconvenience to commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In total, about 620 ground staff were deployed at the affected stations on the first day of service disruption, to assist commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These included SMRT and LTA staff who provided directions and assisted commuters, traffic marshals who facilitated traffic flow, and Police Officers who helped with crowd management.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Caring Commuter Champions – these are commuters who volunteer to help fellow commuters – also assisted by providing directions at some of the bus stops.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Priority was given to seniors, people with difficulty walking and students who were sitting for examinations to board the buses and shuttle trains.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Given the scale of the disruption, there was some initial confusion on the ground when the incident first occurred, and shuttle train services and bridging buses had to be activated.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Operators and workers quickly adapted and stepped up to respond to the situation to mitigate the impact on commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) was due to commence the next day, LTA and the Singapore Examinations and Assessment Board (SEAB) discussed and put in place contingency arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are existing arrangements which students have been briefed on.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, SEAB publicly reassured students that they would not be penalised if they were late due to the disruption and would be given the full allotted time to complete their exams.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Meanwhile, LTA and SMRT engineers were assessing the damage and conducting repair works on the track.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The engineers determined that some pieces of trackside signalling and power equipment had to be replaced.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a safety precaution, LTA and SMRT checked all the axle boxes of the first-generation KHI trains overnight and ensured that they passed the inspection checks before they were put into service the next day.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the second day of the disruption, 26 September, free regular buses and bridging buses resumed at the start of revenue services at 5.00 am, with 80 bridging buses deployed during the morning peak.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Overnight, SMRT, LTA and other bus operators had set up queue poles, signages and other equipment to better direct commuters to the bridging buses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SMRT and LTA also arranged for chartered taxis to provide free rides for students and teachers travelling to PSLE examination venues from Jurong East, Clementi, Dover and Buona Vista stations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This service was similarly provided for those travelling to their PSLE or GCE "N" level examination venues on 27 and 30 September.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By the evening of Thursday, 26 September, given the extensive damage to the tracks and trackside equipment, LTA and SMRT determined that the repairs could be completed only over the weekend.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We informed the public at around 10.00 pm that we aimed to restore services on Monday, 30 September.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For the next two days, Friday and Saturday, the workers continued to carry out the repair works day and night.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On Mr Edward Chia's question about safety for workers, the works were paused during inclement weather.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: All workers were also equipped with personal protection equipment, provided food and drinks, and followed a shift system to ensure that they received adequate rest.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Repair works were completed on Saturday, 28 September.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These cracks could be due to the rail segments being weakened earlier by the incident train when it was being moved back to Ulu Pandan Depot.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If I may use a Chinese Kungfu analogy, it is like sustaining internal injuries that are not immediately visible from the outside and showing symptoms a while later.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The 10 rail segments with these new cracks needed to be replaced before service could safely resume, which meant that an additional day of works was required, including for the thorough testing and inspection after repairs had been completed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The engineers and technicians from LTA and SMRT continued to work through Sunday, 29 September, to replace the affected rail segments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Comprehensive testing of the rail and track equipment then followed that same night and continued on Monday, 30 September, to ensure the integrity of the repaired systems.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Throughout the entire recovery process, safety for our commuters and workers was the team's top priority and thorough testing and checks were conducted to ensure all safety requirements were met before resuming train services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For the first few days of operations, SMRT imposed temporary speed restrictions and operated westbound trains at a slower speed of 40 kilometres per hour, rather than the usual speed of up to 80 kilometres per hour, along the stretch of replaced rail segments.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is part of the standard process following rail replacements, to ensure safety for commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Syed Harun asked whether there are concerns about further rail fractures.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have done a comprehensive series of tests, including endurance tests, before resuming train services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: After the resumption of service, SMRT stepped up its checks as a precautionary measure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is also a regular inspection regime in place for other rail segments, including for other Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines operated by SMRT and SBS Transit.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Several Members have asked about the root cause of the incident.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The severity of this disruption was due to the extensive damage to the track and trackside equipment by the incident train.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As to the root cause, including why the axle box dropped, as well as learning points to improve our responses and prevent future incidents, these are issues which the investigations will cover.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked if the Government would convene a Committee of Inquiry for this incident.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As rail regulator, LTA has the necessary regulatory powers and technical knowledge to investigate serious rail incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA will conduct a thorough investigation to ascertain the root cause of the axle box failure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will also examine the fault detection and incident handling procedures to determine if appropriate actions were taken.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Ministry of Transport's (MOT's) Transport Safety Investigation Bureau (TSIB) will also be conducting an independent safety investigation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA will mete out penalties if the investigations reveal lapses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are a few clarifications which I would like to make in response to Members' questions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Dennis Tan asked about their operations and maintenance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The structural integrity of the trains was assessed by an independent assessor in 2012, who concluded that the trains have a total service life of 38 years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The reliability of a train depends on several factors and not only on its age alone.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Trains that remain reliable can continue to be used, if they have not exceeded their service life.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Prior to 2016, all the trains were owned and operated by the rail operators.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2016, LTA began taking ownership of rail operating assets as part of the transition to the New Rail Financing Framework (NRFF).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Under the NRFF, LTA is responsible for procuring and building up assets, such as the train fleet, while rail operators are responsible for maintaining, deploying and operating the assets.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2018 and 2020, after discussions with SMRT, LTA purchased a total of 106 new R151 trains to replace the North-South and East-West Lines' earliest generations of trains, including the KHI fleet.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The delivery of these trains, however, was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These trains have been arriving in batches, after rigorous testing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The first batch of three trains was handed over to SMRT and put into service in June 2023.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Since then, LTA has been progressively handing over new R151 trains to SMRT, at a rate of about two trains per month.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Thirty-four R151 trains have been handed over to SMRT so far.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, I want to address the questions from Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Ms Hazel Poa about compensation for affected commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Bridging bus services and regular bus services along this stretch were also provided at no cost to commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: SimplyGo has been processing refunds in cases where commuters were charged for two journeys instead of one, due to them exceeding 45 minutes for transfers between train and bus services, or between different bus services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Commuters may approach SimplyGo for assistance if they have specific queries about their fares.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, while I will separately reply to questions on the Fare Review Exercise filed by Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Neil Parekh and Ms Poh Li San, I would like to address Mr Gerald Giam's question about whether this incident and service levels can be taken into consideration in the Fare Review Exercise by the Public Transport Council (PTC).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Please allow me to explain why we should separate service levels and disruptions from how we set public transport fares.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PTC had previously studied whether fare reviews should be linked to service levels and disruptions and decided not to adopt this approach, as there are other measures in place to ensure service standards are met.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For service disruptions, LTA would establish the cause and accountability and mete out penalties where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, when operators do not meet reliability targets, they will also not receive payments under our incentive schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The purpose of the annual Fare Review Exercise is to ensure that fares keep pace with changes in operating costs, so that the public transport system remains financially sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PTC would consider changes in cost drivers over the previous year, based on the fare formula.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Fares are collected for the entire public transport system, including buses and trains, to ensure that the public transport system remains financially sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If our fares are not adjusted to reflect rising operating costs, the persistent shortfall would have a chronic impact on service quality and reliability over time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Or if we want to continue topping-up the shortfall via Government subsidies, it means that taxpayers would have to foot a higher bill.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This requirement applies to both rail operators should they encounter a disruption along their respective lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, as regulator, LTA imposes stringent safety standards, aligned to international best practices that operators must comply with.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Operators who do not meet these standards will be subject to penalties and, where necessary, they will face additional regulatory conditions and monitoring.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, to ensure that equipment and systems remain safe and reliable over time, LTA imposes Maintenance Performance Standards (MPS) under the operator's licence, which set out the requirements that the operator must fulfil in relation to maintenance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are maintenance audits by independent external assessors to ensure operators' compliance with their maintenance regime.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Members, including Mr Ong Hua Han and Mr Dennis Tan, have asked about the maintenance regime for trains.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In general, regular maintenance activities are both time-bound and dependent on mileage.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These can range from regular visual inspections to more elaborate component replacement activities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ad hoc maintenance activities are also carried out if there are abnormal indicators being picked up in between maintenance cycles.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Louis Chua and Mr Saktiandi asked about predictive maintenance capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Where feasible, operators have installed condition-monitoring systems on the trackside and on trains to detect potential defects.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Special vehicles are also used to scan the tracks to pick up issues.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On Mr Saktiandi's question of whether these systems could have detected risks leading up to this incident, these are part of the ongoing investigations and I will not comment further at this point.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, redundancies are built into systems, where feasible, to ensure safety even during incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about redundancy in our power supply system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The trains are powered by the third rail.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are back-up power sources to supply power to the third rail.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If the third rail is damaged and the train cannot move, the on-board battery system will maintain emergency lighting, ventilation fans and public address systems.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Fourth, we have processes in place to respond to incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During a breakdown, if the fault cannot be immediately or easily resolved, the top priority is to detrain commuters to ensure their safety.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As far as possible, the operator will try to let commuters safely alight at the platform.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Where this is not possible, there are procedures in place for detrainment onto the tracks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Staff onboard the train will deploy the detrainment door and guide all passengers to proceed safely to the nearest station platform.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These procedures are consistently applied across all our rail lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Staff undergo regular hands-on training and exercises so that they are familiar with the procedures and well-prepared to handle emergencies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2012, the mean kilometres between failure (MKBF) for the MRT network, which is a reliability benchmark used by cities globally, was 67,000 train-kilometres.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This increased steadily over the decade as LTA worked with rail operators to enhance their maintenance regimes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is comparable to the most reliable overseas metros.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked if we could publish the MKBF figures for our MRT network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Dennis Tan also asked if we utilise MKBF statistics to determine how we exercise oversight over individual lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While all our MRT lines have met the one million MKBF target, each MRT line has its own characteristics, such as their age and whether they are under- or over-ground.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Their systems would also have been commissioned or renewed at different times.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But the key is that all the lines have met our target of at least one million MKBF and we are subjecting them to stringent maintenance and operational standards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These reliability standards are the result of the hard work by our operators and workers over more than a decade.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Since 2011, LTA has been working with rail operators to enhance their maintenance regime.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA has also upgraded signalling and power systems and invested in infrastructure, such as signalling simulation centres, to improve our operators' ability to diagnose and remedy different faults.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The renewal of the six core systems of the North-South and East-West lines is another major project which has helped to improve our reliability standards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA's monitoring of MKBF and licensing conditions also continue to ensure that operators invest sufficiently in maintenance to minimise disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA conducts regular training and information exchange sessions with overseas railway operators and technical experts to ensure that in-house engineering and technical capabilities are aligned with the latest standards and best practices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While we have made significant progress over the last decade, it continues to be a work-in-progress and where we can do better, we will work together with our tripartite partners to implement the improvements.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During service disruptions, we seek commuters' understanding that travel times will be longer.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we will do our best to keep disruptions to a minimum and offer alternative travel options, where possible.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, our public transport network, with six MRT lines together with a sizeable fleet of buses, is more resilient and better able to cope with disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the whole, the mitigation measures across the six days enabled most commuters to continue with their journeys, albeit with additional travelling time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The system was also able to cope throughout the disruption, thanks to the strong efforts by our bus operators and staff on the ground supporting crowd and queue management.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: LTA will press on with the planned expansions in our rail network over the next decade.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will increase our capacity to meet daily commuter travel demand, provide more transport options and further improve our rail resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By the early 2030s, the Cross Island Line will significantly improve connectivity among the West, East and North-East regions in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With almost half of its stations as interchanges, commuters island-wide will have more alternative travel routes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes commuters in the West, who will be able to access the Cross Island Line via the Jurong Lake District, West Coast and Clementi stations and connect to every other radial line in our MRT network.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the mid-2030s, the new Sungai Kadut interchange station between the North-South Line and the Downtown Line will provide commuters in the North-West a more direct transfer to the Downtown Line.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These additions to our network will enhance rail connectivity and resilience, especially in the West, and better connect the Western Region to other parts of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Members have suggested that buses could be used to improve resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our public bus network plays a key role in complementing our rail network, providing first-mile and last-mile connectivity within towns and bringing commuters to key transport nodes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They provide some resilience and alternative routes during rail disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That is why, even when we need to rationalise bus services, we retain at least one trunk route that runs parallel to MRT lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also have the Bus Connectivity Enhancement Programme, which will further improve bus services, especially to new estates and those located further away from major transport nodes and town centres.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That said, buses cannot fully replace rail capacity in the event of a rail disruption, even with the injection of bridging buses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Rail is still the most efficient mode of public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A six-car train on the East-West Line can carry more than 1,000 commuters and runs at a two-to-three minute intervals during peak hours and at speeds of up to 80 kilometres per hour.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During the disruption from 25 to 30 September, alternative routes using other MRT lines and regular bus services were necessary too.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Indeed, there was a recent Business Times commentary on how flexible work arrangements can be helpful during major transport disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will discuss the idea further with employers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Members would recall that a decade or so ago, we faced significant challenges in the quality and reliability of our MRT service.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The entire public transport sector and all stakeholders, including our unions, workers, operators and Government, then came together and worked very hard to significantly improve our MRT connectivity and reliability over the past decade.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While we do our best to avoid disruptions, incidents may still happen from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What is important is how we respond to the incidents and how we learn from them to strengthen our resilience against future disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The safety of commuters was paramount, which was why we took the necessary time to complete the repairs and conduct rigorous testing before safely resuming services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They have the technical expertise to do so and LTA will be further supported by the experience of the EAP.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will learn from this episode, remain vigilant and work closely with our tripartite partners to continually improve our public transport system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, I would like to say a big thank you to our public transport workers and caring commuter volunteers for their hard work and dedication to safely restore full train services, to provide bridging bus services to ferry commuters and to assist commuters on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We greatly appreciate your commitment and professionalism and how many of you went beyond the call of duty and worked together as a cohesive team to overcome the challenges and help commuters with their journeys.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, I wish to thank our commuters and the public for their patience and their understanding and for showing care and concern to our staff.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It was heartening to know that some of our commuters penned words of encouragement for our workers and brought them food and drinks, which boosted their morale and lifted their spirits.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Your acts of kindness were very much appreciated by our workers and our volunteers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):   After the MRT disruption, Shin Min Daily News published a letter describing the spirit demonstrated by Singaporeans during this incident.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The letter said: "This MRT disruption was a test for us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But it also gave us the opportunity to recognise the most valuable resource in our city – our people.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is our people, with their grit and dedication, who have made our city what it is today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The next time we are enjoying a convenient ride on the MRT, let us not forget the workers who are toiling silently in the background – it was through their hard work that we built up a strong and resilient nation.” Mr Speaker, through the close cooperation of the tripartite partners, our public transport system has seen significant improvements over the past decade.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, we know there is still room for improvement.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will work together with our tripartite partners to do our utmost to make our public transport system safer, more reliable and more resilient. : Mr Speaker, the true resilience goes beyond the number of MRT lines or bus services that we operate; it rests in the strength and resolve of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the midst of this difficult period, it was heartening to see many Singaporeans stepping forward to encourage our workers and to support one another.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In my Mandarin speech earlier, I quoted from a letter published by Shin Min Daily News on 1 October.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The unofficial translation reads: “This MRT disruption was a test for us.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But it also gave us the opportunity to recognise the most valuable resource in our city – our people.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is our people, with their grit and dedication, who have made our city what it is today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The next time we are enjoying a convenient ride on the MRT, let us not forget the workers who are toiling silently in the background – it was through their hard work that we built up a strong and resilient nation.” Sir, this is a beautiful tribute to the dedication of our workers and the resilience of our nation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Just as Singaporeans rallied together during previous challenges, once again, as a community and a society, we came together to overcome this challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The public transport community has come a long way in our journey to developing a safe, reliable and resilient rail system.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now have clarifications on the Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call on Members, I would like to take this opportunity to remind Members that pursuant to Standing Order 23, Members may seek clarification on the Ministerial Statement, but there is no debate that should be allowed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, Members can seek clarification by way of asking questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Likewise, I also ask the Minister to also keep his answers clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are a total of 21 Members who had filed Parliamentary Questions (PQs) for oral or written answer on this matter.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will give priority to these Members first.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will not give a speech, Mr Speaker, but allow me this opportunity to join in to thank the "One Transport Family", they have worked together as one transport family, volunteers and staff, as the Minister has mentioned, Singaporeans coming in to join in to help out, over the six days.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, really, thanks to all of them for making sure that it was solved within six days.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is in regard to rail reliability and trying to find the right balance between rail reliability and the cost of maintaining service levels.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is something that I have asked in my PQ slated for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have noticed that there have been comments on social media that the East-West Line disruption occurred because the Chairman of SMRT had claimed in June 2023 that they did not want over-maintenance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can I seek the Minister's views on this and if the Minister can also share about our relations, in terms of the One Transport Family with our rail operators?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in summary, how is the balance struck between the cost of over-maintenance and the prevention of avoidable disruption incidents?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Lastly, before I end, I would like to thank the Minister for answering my preventive maintenance question.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think they would appreciate it very much.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: His main point was about striking a balance between achieving high reliability standards and incurring high maintenance costs, to achieve what he described as "optimal maintenance".

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA colleagues and I understand where Mr Seah is coming from and we agree with his sensible and balanced approach.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are indeed important trade-offs that we need to look at between achieving high reliability standards while keeping the overall maintenance costs sustainable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: SMRT has also invested in building up its engineering and technical capabilities under Mr Seah's chairmanship and it has embarked on initiatives using its own resources to further improve rail reliability.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Allow me to say that these can be rather misleading, because they selectively quoted certain comments rather than reflect the full context and the full story.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, Mr Seah had said, and this was reported by the mainstream media in 2023, that SMRT would, in his words, "never want to under-maintain" because he wanted to avoid the reliability issues of the past.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, Sir, this is an example to remind ourselves of the importance of understanding the full context, what happened, so that we do not get misled by certain social media posts or comments and then we arrive at the wrong conclusions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And secondly, with respect to the damage caused by the fallen axle, such a degree of damage could not have been done silently.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There must have been quite a bit of noise.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, can the Minister shed light on why it was not discovered earlier but instead allowed to drag on for over two kilometres of the track?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I covered it briefly in my Statement earlier, that this was one of the bogies of one of the cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Each car has two sets of these bogies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As to exactly why the falling of the axle box and then the bogie shifting off the rails did not result in the discovery earlier, I think that is a subject of the investigations and we will await the investigation findings to ascertain what happened.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Poa also asked about the difference between the different approaches.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, the one that is done by TSIB, which focuses on safety investigations, would be different from the one that LTA is doing, because LTA, as regulator, would also have to look at whether there are any lapses and to decide whether any penalties need to be mete out.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there are differences in different types of investigations, but what is common across all the different approaches is that they will be thorough, they will be evidence-based and they will focus on finding out what happened, ascertaining what are the root causes and then identifying where are the areas for improvement.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My clarification surrounds the issue of how we can minimise the inconvenience caused to our commuters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, can the Ministry share what are the key feedback received thus far?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second clarification pertains to, first of all, I think we should applaud those who stepped forward, based on what the Minister has shared about how the crisis management team has come forward to render assistance to our children who are studying for exams, as well as seniors and those with mobility issues.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But apart from this category of commuters, whether the Ministry or the LTA's crisis management response teams have also looked into how we should also reach out as soon as possible to mommies who are expecting and those that are accompanied by young children as well, to prioritise reaching out to them and render the necessary assistance at the earliest opportunity?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my humble opinion, it is not common for our train system to break down to such a substantive extent, in which it has affected millions of commuters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, it seems to me as a form of national crisis and as what the Minister has said, it has involved multiple stakeholders to come together, united as one Singapore, to reach out and resolve these issues.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, in this regard, is this an appropriate situation where we should activate and test out the efforts that we have harnessed through our Total Defence and also our SGSecure activities, where communities have previously experienced crisis management exercises, for these stakeholders to also be activated?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think certainly this is something that we do regularly, to gather feedback and identify areas for improvement after every incident, whether big or small.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I mentioned in my statement earlier, because of the scale of the disruption, on the first day, I think there was some confusion on the ground.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But to give credit to the response teams and to the ground officers and volunteers, they saw where these gaps are and then they adapted quickly to improve the arrangements.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And on the first day, towards the later part, and the second day onwards, the processes and arrangements got better.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, they incorporated what they learnt from previous incidents and they also adapted to what is happening on the ground during this incident.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And I am glad Ms Soh also acknowledged the hard work that our staff have put in and I thank Ms Soh for that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Soh's second question about different groups of commuters, certainly, that is an area that we will continually finetune and improve.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Certainly, we will look out for this group of commuters to see how we can extend a helping hand.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The third question, I have no doubt that our Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) colleagues are ready and willing to help.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is what they are trained for, to respond to crises.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I am also mindful that unless it is really necessary, we should not take them away from their primary responsibilities of defending the country.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And if it is something that we are still able to cope within the transport ecosystem, we should try and do that first.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Also because, our officers and our volunteers have gone through regular rehearsals and exercises to train for this type of scenario.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when it happens, they are also more familiar with the operating environment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They are also more able to see what the best way is to respond to help commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We were still able to assist commuters to complete their journeys.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I have two supplementary questions and the Minister has touched on the first one in his response to Ms Hany Soh.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: First, train disruptions are often a chaotic and confusing experience for commuters.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Persons with disabilities (PWDs) and the elderly are particularly vulnerable and in need of help, as they may not know who to turn to in unfamiliar situations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Given this, may I ask the Minister to consider additional training for ground staff to better equip themselves to identify and proactively offer support to our more vulnerable commuters?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Second, some commuters were unaware of the train faults until they arrived at the MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For PWDs and seniors who meticulously plan their commute, this can be quite disruptive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is, can the Minister share details on SMRT's performance against the new maintenance performance standards set up by LTA as part of the new NRFF, which the Minister also mentioned, what these key performance indicators (KPIs) are and whether SMRT has been able to meet all of them?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Because I also noticed that if we look at MKBF statistics, it has been consistently lower than that of SBS Transit.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even so, if we consider that the North-East Line, for example, is older than the Circle Line.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second question is that, can the Minister share the dollar amounts for maintenance-related expenditures for SMRT in the last three years and also as a percentage of its rail fare revenues and how has this trended since the NRFF, especially after comments by its Chairman in June that it does not want both under- and over-maintenance, which Minister also referenced, just so that we can set out the full numbers and context here?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The maintenance and the overall reliability outcomes as shown by MKBF, I have explained earlier as well that different lines have different ages, different operating environments, run different systems.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, while there is indeed a difference in the MKBF numbers across different lines, including between the different lines operated by the same company – SBS Transit, the two lines that they operate; SMRT, the lines that they operate – I would say the more important thing is this and that was what Mr Louis Chua was trying to drive at: where do we strike that balance between reliability and maintenance?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That will put us in the league of the best-performing metros around the world.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You can say, why not two million; why not four or five million?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Nothing to stop you from setting that target.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I hope Mr Chua will agree with me that we also have to ask that question: if you were to set that target, instead of setting a target of one million, we raise it to, say, four million, five million, we also got to ask, what is the cost incurred by the system as a whole, which will then translate into cost for commuters, cost for taxpayers, to achieve those standards.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is where the balance needs to be struck.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It does not mean that we should take that for granted or become complacent.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We should continue to work hard and if we see that Circle Line, for example, is not doing as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, among all the lines at the moment, that is the one with the lowest MKBF.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is ongoing work being done to try and improve the systems, to upgrade for the Circle Line, including closing the circle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we believe once those works are completed over the next couple of years, it will help to improve the overall reliability for Circle Line as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When we look at the amount that they are spending, they have both continued to focus on maintenance and on building up the engineering and technical expertise, which is equally important.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is something which will remain a priority for LTA and the operators.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am also surprised to hear that there are 12 new cracks found on unreplaced tracks.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is to prevent a recurrence before the EAP puts up its report.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan's second point, I just want to highlight that it is not only after an incident that LTA will conduct audits and checks.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is something that is ongoing and for all the lines and for both operators.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But what we did, together with the operator, after this incident was to step up additional checks because when you have a big disruption and you replace the rail, you do need to do some additional checks to ensure safety.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Putting aside the additional checks for the affected segments of the rail, the ongoing work to conduct regular checks, that is something that takes place regularly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to thank all the workers and volunteers and all the ancillary personnel, like drivers, bus drivers, taxi drivers, who have helped with the service recovery in the six days during the disruption.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I had Question No 17 from yesterday's Order paper.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am not sure whether the Minister has answered that question or is this subject to the outcome of the investigation by the various bodies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My second clarification, pending the outcome of the investigation by the various committees' personnel, whether any additional interim maintenance measures have been put in place or will be put in place so as to prevent similar incidents from happening in the meantime.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But if I recall correctly, it has to do with the causes of the accident.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Dennis Tan, you may want to clarify.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Yes, Mr Speaker, I think it is quicker if I were to just read out the question: To ask the Minister for Transport whether LTA will conduct a review of the existing requirement on the maintenance regime and practices of all MRT trains, including but not limited to the old trains, such as the first-generation KHI trains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I am not asking any follow-up questions on my Parliamentary Questions relating to the cause and the faults, pending the outcome of the investigation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: He filed a number of questions and as he pointed out, some relating to the investigations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On maintenance on the old trains, I did highlight earlier as well, that because the investigations will cover the maintenance regime for KHI trains and see whether that is something that is a possible reason for the incident.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Pending the investigation outcomes, I also, likewise, seek Mr Tan's understanding that I would not be able to comment on that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the important point is this: we do not wait for an incident to happen, before we do the necessary checks on the systems and the processes together with the operators.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, LTA looks at both what are the outcomes and also whether the systems and processes are in place.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These checks are being done regularly for all the lines and it is ongoing work.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I explained earlier in response to Mr Lim Biow Chuan's question, after an incident were to happen, of course, there is heightened alert during that period; you do want to put in some extra checks because you do want to take some additional precautionary measures.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But it does not mean that, therefore, we do not do these regular checks on the other lines and on a regular basis.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also would like to join the Minister and other colleagues to thank all the workers and volunteers and also the public for putting in effort to help solve these problems.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, I read from the social media that some people have asked why there were still the axle box failures, despite the spending on the renewal the North-South and East-West lines.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also want to ask the Minister, does he expect this amount to be increased further after this incident?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Under this programme, we renewed and enhanced six core systems of the North-South and East-West Lines: the rail sleepers, the third rail, signalling, power supply, track circuit and also the purchase of new trains to replace the older trains.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this renewal programme was needed to ensure that the services on these older lines can continue to operate reliably for years to come.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I hope that addresses the point that Mr Gan raised.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to thank all the engineers and technicians who had worked day and night and sometimes under extremely bad weather to get the East-West Line, west of Jurong East Station operational again.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the bus drivers, public transport workers and volunteers who responded to the call for help.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In order not to subject them to another such incident, it is important that we investigate this incident thoroughly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, I have two supplementary questions for the Minister regarding the COI.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, I think many Singaporeans would like the Minister to explain the difference between this breakdown and the 2011 breakdown when a COI was called, and what made the Minister conclude that these two breakdowns are different, and a COI is not required this time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Leong asked what is the difference between this incident and 2011 is.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Today, as I shared earlier, all the lines are above our target of at least one million MKBF.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In 2011, the incident that happened, the context and the situation were not the same.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Leong may remember in between 2011 and now, we also had other serious MRT-related incidents: there was a flooding at Bishan; there was an incident at Joo Koon.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And for those incidents, we did not convene a COI, but LTA conducted a thorough investigation for each of them and then learned from what happened to see how we can improve.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I mentioned earlier, this does not mean that we think we have arrived and therefore become complacent.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But based on our assessment, LTA has, as regulator, the necessary expertise and powers to conduct a thorough investigation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I declare I work in a global investment firm that owns one of our rail operators.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First is, I am glad to hear that the Ministry has outlined the steps taken to address the recent disruptions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But given these disruptions, can the Ministry share whether a comprehensive review of the entire MRT network is deemed necessary at this point in time?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And second, how would these breakdowns in services impact on the Government's effort to promote a car-lite society and encourage reliance on rail transport?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And I shared in my Statement earlier that we are continuing to invest heavily in building up new MRT infrastructure, new lines – the Cross Island Line, the Jurong Region Line – upgrading existing lines, not just the North-South, East-West Lines, but also Circle Line, completing the circle.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We still have an ongoing project with Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have opened up phase four to Marine Parade area, but there is still some more to go.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And our commitment to providing a safe, reliable and resilient MRT system, that also remains unchanged.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, were any of the new trains delivered but not immediately put into service?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How then will commuters be assured that fare increases will lead to tangible improvements in service reliability?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, how much of the fare revenue increased is allocated specifically towards improving service reliability?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is still within their service life, and they will be replaced before that 38-year service mark is reached.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Can we speed up on the new trains to try and catch up on the delays due to COVID-19 earlier?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is certainly something that we will do our best to meet, but I also hope Mr Giam agrees we need to do so without compromising safety.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the trains that come will have to be tested thoroughly before they are put into service.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I do not think there is any disagreement on can we speed up and whether we are able to do so, to do some catching up due to the delays caused by COVID-19, but to do so in a manner which is safe.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The second question from Mr Giam, I think I have explained my reasons.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there are incentives for the operator to improve their reliability and to maintain a high level of service quality.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we were to incorporate this element into fares, and as I said, I understand where Mr Giam and some members of the public are coming from.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I understand and I respect your point of view, Mr Giam, but there are some downsides to doing that as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you say, "No, let us not do that, let us ask Government to provide a top-up", then effectively we are asking taxpayers to fund the shortfall.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there are some trade-offs and the PTC, after considering the different perspectives, decided that we will separate the two things, but to hold the operators accountable and to incentivise them to achieve high reliability standards through other ways.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to declare that many Clementi residents living around Clementi MRT station and the affected segment were badly affected.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some were, themselves, transport workers and later on were working late through the night, together with colleagues across Singapore, to restore service.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If you looked down from some of the high-rise blocks in Clementi, you could see the workers working through the night.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Residents were circulating videos as a message of encouragement to one another to pull together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have got two clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The first is, I note that the Ministerial Statement starts out with a very important operative word: safe.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister continue to assure us that as we review our transport system, safety will continue to be the first priority – safety for passengers, safety for workers, safety for the public?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Indeed, that is a top priority for all of us in the transport family.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When we were doing the repair works, of course, everyone wanted to complete the repair works as quickly as possible.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But from the Government agencies to the operators to the unions, I think we are all on the same page, that we should do so safely, ensuring safety for our workers and ensuring safety for commuters and the public.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if we need to take more time to do thorough testing, to carry out the repair works properly, we will explain to the public why more time is needed, but never compromise on safety.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are also grateful to the public, to our commuters, for their kind understanding and their patience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think people agreed with the point that Dr Tan Wu Meng was making, that safety must come first.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Safety for our workers, safety for commuters and the public.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will ensure that regardless of the outcomes of the investigations, we want to continue to maintain this environment whereby safety is a top priority.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We also want to continue to have an environment, together with our tripartite partners, to encourage our workers, as Dr Tan suggested, to speak up when they see that something is not safe, something needs to be changed and improved.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first relates to a part of the PQ that I filed for yesterday, where I asked, what was the total capacity of bridging bus services put into effect, compared to the average ridership of the stations that were closed as part of this disruption.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Minister mentioned that bridging bus services cannot match the train in terms of speed and capacity, even with 80 buses deployed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I am wondering whether he has figures on what was the capacity of the actual bridging bus services that were deployed?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The second one relates to safety, which we just talked about.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As with other Members of the House, I would like to extend my gratitude to the workers and everyone on the ground who worked hard to get our rail system up and running again.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I wanted to come back to this and ask the Minister, what specific measures were taken during this incident to ensure that the workers working around the clock to effect repairs, including those workers who were working for contractors, were working safely, including not working double or additional shifts beyond what is safe?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Were there, for example, advisories or directives that the Ministry or LTA actually issued to the workers and contractors to tell them what the avenues and measures that are available to them?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You can do a simple multiplication and you can compare that with the train capacity during normal operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That will help to absorb a large proportion of the affected load due to the disruption.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Then, buses will come in to supplement this, to provide additional capacity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Buses have their roles because they are more nimble, they are more flexible.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why we need to continue to invest in expanding our rail network, including in the western part of Singapore where there are ongoing projects.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On Ms He's second question, I covered it earlier as well in my Statement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is not something that we need to impose because there are already ongoing efforts by the operator, by the unions to, during normal times, emphasise the importance of safety and letting this become part of the culture of the organisation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when a crisis happens, those instincts, those muscles kick in very naturally and the support systems are there, the measures are there, to take care of the workers and ensure their safety while they work.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But what was a bonus for our workers was that – we did not plan for this, but it came as a positive, pleasant surprise to our workers – it was the very encouraging support from commuters and members of the public.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This was spontaneous, ground-up acts of kindness shown by our commuters and the public to encourage our workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That really lifted their morale and boosted their spirits.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having said that, I do have something to ask the Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We know that it will cost more to have a more reliable, resilient and more connected public transport system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Minister mentioned having more buses that will complement the MRT lines.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, there is a significant role for buses as well, given their agility and reliability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But we also know that there are also competing demands for limited budget resources.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, can I ask the Minister, who is also the Second Minister for Finance, if the Government would also review the overall Government funding and subsidies for public transport so that we can have a more reliable, more resilient as well as more connected public transport system.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are not done upgrading and expanding our public transport system.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On rail, I described earlier in my speech some of the ongoing projects – building of new lines, further expansion of existing lines, upgrading of existing lines.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are a big commitment from a Budget point of view, but we are prepared to make these investments because we can see the benefits that these long-term infrastructural investments can bring in improving connectivity, benefiting commuters from different parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We had explained previously in this House that, where there are buses that experienced a significant drop in ridership because they run parallel to MRT lines and these are usually the long trunk routes, we would have to rationalise some of them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But as I explained earlier, we do not rationalise all because we do want to keep some for redundancy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we do need to adjust and optimise the usage of our scarce resources so that we can redeploy to support the need for new bus services in other areas, including new towns, including new estates in existing towns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I explained in this House previously, doing this alone will not be adequate because we have a programme to build more houses in different parts of Singapore, including in some of the new estates, but also in existing estates but further away from town centres and key transport nodes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have already started with some of the initial new bus services to serve different parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I just want to end off my reply to Mr Liang to reassure Mr Liang and the House that we will continue our investments in our public transport system, both rail and bus.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because we believe that public transport, given our very compact city layout, is the preferred mode of transport for the majority of Singaporeans and it is the preferred mode of transport even for people who own cars.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You do not have to use your car all the time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For certain journeys, you can actually take public transport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We want to encourage an increase in the modal share through public transport.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why we are investing in both rail and bus.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Melvin Yong, I know you have raised your hand for the last 20 minutes, but I had to give priority to all Members who had filed PQs on this first.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I first declare my interest as the Executive Secretary of the National Transport Workers' Union (NTWU).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I therefore thank the Minister and many Members who have stood up to express their recognition and appreciation for our public transport workers, who have worked very hard following the incident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to assure Members that the union takes the safety and welfare of our public transport workers very seriously.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We work very closely with the LTA, the Ministry and the public transport operators, to ensure that their safety and their welfare were never compromised.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the Executive Secretary of NTWU, I can also vouch for the SMRT Chairman, Mr Seah Moon Ming, when he said that there had been no under-investment in maintenance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In fact, our SMRT workers have been working hard, if not harder than ever before, in ensuring that our rail system functions smoothly every day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The MKBF statistics that the Minister has highlighted can testify to the improvements in rail reliability over the years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, my question relates to maintenance, in addition to the hefty investments in rail replacement projects, part of the success in maintaining this high MKBF threshold can be attributed to investments in predictive maintenance tools and systems.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And beyond systems, how have LTA and SMRT invested in developing our engineering and technical talent to ensure that our MRT remains safe and reliable for all of us?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But if I may comment, generally, on the approach taken by both operators, not just SMRT, but also SBS Transit, on using predictive maintenance, condition monitoring.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The idea there is this: you want to use sensors and analytics to pick up faults that are going to occur, but have yet to occur.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In other words, picking them up before they may become problems that will cause disruptions, and then you can intervene early – prevention is better than cure – and then to either replace that part or to carry out some additional servicing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the idea of condition monitoring or predictive maintenance is a correct one.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And it will help to improve overall service quality and reliability.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But as to whether that was adequate, or that was effectively carried out in this particular incident, as I have explained earlier, we await the findings of the investigation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Melvin Yong also asked about engineering talent and, Sir, that is crucial.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we do not build up the engineering and technical expertise, you can have good hardware, good systems, whether predictive maintenance or otherwise, you will not be able to make good use of them and you would not be able to keep on improving the processes, and to improve safety, reliability and resilience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, talent development is a key part of our overall strategy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is a key priority for LTA and our operators, especially when we need to operate and maintain an expanding and increasingly complex rail system.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we adopt a multi-pronged approach towards building up the talent pool and capabilities of our rail sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: SMRT, for example, would train its engineering staff through courses conducted by the original equipment manufacturers, or OEMs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And also they have a SMRT Institute that is set up to conduct the training for their staff.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The training syllabus is constantly reviewed and updated, based on lessons learned and experiences gained during actual operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The LTA, too, has established the Singapore Rail Academy in 2017.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Academy works together with the Institutes of Higher Learning and they provide relevant training for engineers within the sector in key knowledge areas, such as rail engineering, operations and maintenance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And in terms of incentives that can help to augment the existing programmes, LTA, together with the rail operators, and also with the unions, NTWU, introduced the Rail Manpower Development Package in 2019, which has three components.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, incentives that encourage the operators to further expand and accelerate their training programmes in areas, such as data analytics, robotics and automation, and condition-based monitoring.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And third, there are grants to support investments in training hardware, such as equipment and simulators.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These were provided to enhance the training for our workers, make it more realistic, make it more productive for our workers to undergo training.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The staff from LTA and the two rail operators also participate in regular exchanges with overseas operators, including the Hong Kong Mass Transit Railway and the Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation, to learn from international best practices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is an area, as I mentioned earlier, that LTA will continue to work closely with our tripartite partners to equip our workers, including our engineering and technical workers, with the necessary skills to stay relevant and to stay productive as we expand our rail network.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Beyond already announced rail projects, when will LTA implement the previously announced West Coast extension, to create more rail resiliency in the West region, where there are fewer rail alternatives compared to the other regions of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are pressing on with plan expansions in our rail network over the next decade.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I mentioned some of this in my Statement earlier: Jurong Region Line and the Cross-Island Line.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And these will help to enhance rail connectivity and resilience, especially in the West, and it will help to better connect the western region to other parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond these expansions to the Jurong Region Line and the Cross-Island Line, LTA will continue to plan for the future and to ensure that our rail network is well connected and resilient.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: LTA's studies include working with the relevant planning agencies to assess the demand and implementation timeline of the project, to support further developments in the West.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And should the study show that it is feasible to proceed with this extension, it will help to further improve rail connectivity between the western parts of Singapore and the city centre.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will also help to support further developments in the West, and importantly, it will help to enhance the overall resilience of our rail network.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I was given to understand that under a COI, it allows for the public hearing of inputs from experts, rather than reading about it in a summarised version in a report.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It has been a good two hours on the Ministerial Statement.
